:::: {.tb-prose}

## What is TakwimuBridge?

TakwimuBridge is designed to help a researcher analyse information collected through interviews, Key Informant Interviews (KIIs), Focus Group Discussions (FGDs), open-ended questions and other written qualitative information.

You do not need to be an advanced data analyst to use it. You mainly need to read the information, identify important ideas, highlight them, and classify them into themes. TakwimuBridge then helps organize, count, compare and present those findings.

## A Simple Example

Suppose you interviewed five people about challenges facing their community. Each interview produced about three pages of written information.

You create a new project and upload the five interviews. You tell the system whether each document is a KII, FGD, interview, open-ended response, or another document.

You open the first interview and start reading. A respondent might say: *"One of our biggest problems is pollution because industries are discharging waste into the river."*

You decide that this statement is talking about **Environmental Pollution**. You highlight the statement and select or create the theme *Environmental Pollution*. You may choose yellow as its colour. TakwimuBridge automatically records that Environmental Pollution has been mentioned once.

If another respondent discusses pollution, you highlight that statement using the same theme. The frequency becomes two. You continue doing this across all interviews.

::: {.callout-note}
This exact example — five KIIs plus one FGD discussing environmental pollution, water scarcity, poor planning and unemployment — is bundled into TakwimuBridge as the **demo project** on the [Projects](projects.html) page, already fully coded for its *Challenges*, *Causes* and *Impacts*, so you can see the finished result before coding your own data.
:::

## Giving Importance to a Statement

Sometimes two people may discuss the same issue, but the statements may not carry the same weight in your analysis. TakwimuBridge lets you give each highlighted statement an optional score from **1 to 10**.

For example, one Environmental Pollution statement may receive a weight of 8/10, another 6/10, another 9/10. TakwimuBridge can then tell you both how frequently the issue appeared *and* the importance you assigned to the coded statements.

The score represents **your assessment**, as the researcher, of the importance or salience of the statement — it is not automatically the respondent's own numerical rating.

## Creating Different Themes

As you continue reading, different issues will emerge — Environmental Pollution, Water Shortage, Poor Planning, Unemployment, Weak Law Enforcement, and so on.

Every time you find a statement relating to one of these issues, you highlight it and assign the appropriate theme.

You can also organize related issues under broader themes. For example, *Environmental Challenges* may contain *Environmental Pollution*, *Water Shortage* and *Deforestation*. *Governance Challenges* may contain *Poor Planning*, *Weak Enforcement* and *Limited Community Participation*.

## Reading Once, Coding Several Themes

Most studies ask more than one question of the same interviews — for example, *what are the challenges*, *what causes them*, and *what are their impacts*. You should not have to read every transcript three times.

Make one broad theme per question — say **Challenges**, **Causes** and **Impacts** — each with its own sub-themes. In the [Coding Workspace](workspace.html), the coding panel beside the transcript shows all of them at once. Select a passage, then tick every sub-theme it speaks to, from any group:

> *"The factory near the river keeps releasing waste into the water, and nobody stops them."*
> → **Challenges** › Environmental Pollution, **Causes** › Industrial Waste Discharge, **Causes** › Weak Enforcement

One click on **Apply** records all three. If a new idea comes up while you read, add it as a new sub-theme right there in the panel — no need to stop and open the codebook. The highlight in the transcript shows one coloured stripe per theme, and the **Highlight** buttons above the transcript let you show or hide each group.

## What TakwimuBridge Does Automatically

While you concentrate on reading and coding, the software does the counting and organization. For every theme, it calculates:

1. **Frequency** — the number of times it was coded.
2. **Respondent Coverage** — the number and percentage of respondents who mentioned it.
3. **Total Weighted Score** — the sum of the importance scores you assigned.
4. **Average Weight** — the average importance across all references coded under it.

This avoids a common mistake: one person mentioning an issue ten times is different from ten different people each mentioning it once. TakwimuBridge shows both.

You can read these results at the **theme** level (for example, everything coded under *Impacts*) or at the **sub-theme** level (for example, *Health Effects* compared with *Youth Migration*) — switch with the *Themes / Sub-themes* buttons on the [Dashboard](index.html) and [Theme Analysis](analysis.html) pages. A theme counts each coded statement once, even when the statement was coded to two of its sub-themes.

## Seeing What People Actually Said

TakwimuBridge does not only give you numbers. Click a theme, such as *Environmental Pollution*, on the [Theme Analysis](analysis.html) page and it shows every statement you highlighted under that theme, and where it came from — so when writing a report, you can move from a number straight back to the evidence behind it.

## Comparing Different Groups

If you entered basic respondent attributes, TakwimuBridge can compare groups such as Men vs. Women, Youth vs. Adults, Community Members vs. Government Officials, District A vs. District B, or KIIs vs. FGDs — helping you see whether different groups view the same problem differently.

## Creating Graphs and Word Clouds

Bar charts show the most frequently discussed themes. Weighted bar charts show themes with the highest combined importance scores. The **theme cloud** shows your themes sized by how often each was coded, while the **word cloud** shows commonly occurring words, sized by frequency. Heat maps show which themes are more common among different respondents. Comparison charts compare themes between groups.

## Working on More Than One Computer

If accounts are switched on for your site, sign in with **Sign in to sync** at the bottom of the sidebar. Your projects are then kept in your account as well as in the browser, so you can sign in on another computer and carry on. On a shared computer, sign out when you finish — that removes your projects from that browser.

Without an account, projects stay in the browser you used. To move one, use **Export → Full Project Backup (JSON)** and restore it on the other computer.

## The Process in Ten Simple Steps

1. Upload what people said.
2. Read the interviews or discussions.
3. Highlight important statements.
4. Give each statement every theme it speaks to.
5. Give the theme or code a colour.
6. Optionally give the coded statement an importance score from 1–10.
7. TakwimuBridge counts and organizes the coded information.
8. Compare themes and respondents.
9. Create graphs, tables, heat maps and theme or word clouds.
10. Export the findings for your report.

## In Simple Terms

A beginner does not need to understand complicated programming or statistical commands. **You** do the interpretation; TakwimuBridge helps organize, quantify, compare and visualize the qualitative evidence.
